doc.title: Doc Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 28, 1995

title: Roy Hargrove and the young trumpet players
summary: Cheatham follows Roy Hargrove and compares today's players, who hear more, with his own self-made path.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: generation has its influence about jazz, all of us, I’d like to be here 50 more years to hear it.

Yes, I’m very interested in that. I hear a lot of these kids today and I’m surprised to hear what they’re playing. They’re playing so, so pretty and so beautiful, and I wonder where it’s coming from. And now I see where it’s coming from. I follow Roy Hargrove, because he’s such a nice guy — a lot of guys don’t like you to bother them you know — but Roy is very nice and a wonderful player. I follow him. I’m watching him very carefully. Every time I see him there’s something different about his conception of jazz. Very nice, too.
Where do you think his influences were?

Well I’ll tell you, his influences were from all the rest of the young trumpet players of his era. Because they all have the same influence, but with differences among all of them. There is a slight difference with all of us, even old timers, there’s a difference.
You consider yourself an old timer?

Yes, that’s the way it is, and I’m very excited about it because what I went through I don’t think they ever had to go through what I had to go through to become a player, a jazz player. They never had to go through that. Because they can hear more than I heard when I was young. I didn’t hear hardly anything I mean but Louis Armstrong through guys like that, but most of them all sound the same and have the same conception of jazz. They all, back in my day, they were all alike, except Louis Armstrong.
